title: Acute seizure
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise a prolonged convulsive seizure as an emergency and call for help at once.
Know that anticonvulsant medicines are given only as prescribed or per the unit's protocol or the person's emergency plan.
Look for treatable causes such as low glucose and report them.
Seek expert guidance if the first treatment does not work.

sources.use: NICE NG217 chapter 7 (updated August 2026): recommendations 7.1.1 to 7.1.9 on convulsive status epilepticus
FDA lorazepam label: respiratory depression, concomitant opioids
JBDS: hypoglycaemia is an emergency and must be excluded in anyone with seizures

required_sources: First-aid and positioning guidance for an in-hospital seizure from a source read in full (not in NG217 chapter 7)
Critical-care guidance on seizures in sedated or ventilated patients and on electroencephalography
Unit status-epilepticus protocol and the individual patient's emergency plan
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Medicine names, doses, routes and timings in NG217 are deliberately not used; they come from the plan, the order and the unit protocol.
Positioning, protection from injury and observation during the seizure are not in the chapter read and are not written.
NG217 is a UK guideline for children, young people and adults; refractory status epilepticus (third-line treatment and general anaesthesia) is outside this scenario.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
NICE: Notice of rights not read; paraphrase only.
setting: A fictional adult on a fictional ward whose convulsive seizure has not stopped.

steps.info: A patient is having a convulsive seizure that has been going on for several minutes and shows no sign of stopping.

options.text: Call for urgent help, note the time the seizure began, stay with the patient and start emergency care per the unit's protocol, asking for the emergency equipment and prescribed emergency medicine to be brought. Ask a colleague to check bedside glucose in parallel with emergency care, without delaying authorised seizure treatment.
options.feedback: NICE says to provide resuscitation and immediate emergency treatment for a convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more; calling for help and noting the time supports that. Assess potentially reversible causes, including hypoglycaemia, during the initial response rather than waiting for treatment failure.
options.consequence: Help arrives while you stay with the patient and the time of onset is clear.

options.text: Leave the bedside to look for a doctor.
options.feedback: Getting help is right, but leaving the patient removes emergency care at the worst moment.
options.consequence: The patient is alone during the seizure until you return.

options.text: Wait to see whether the seizure stops by itself.
options.feedback: A prolonged convulsive seizure is an emergency that needs immediate treatment.
options.consequence: Treatment is delayed and the seizure continues.

steps.info: The doctor arrives, confirms there is no individual emergency plan, and intravenous access and resuscitation equipment are ready.
steps.prompt: What is the nurse's role regarding the medicine?

options.text: Prepare and give the first-line emergency medicine only as prescribed or as the unit's protocol directs, with resuscitation equipment ready and the patient's breathing watched closely afterwards.
options.feedback: NICE sets out the first-line treatment when no plan is available; which medicine and how much is for the prescriber or protocol, and the lorazepam label warns of respiratory depression, especially with opioids.
options.consequence: The medicine is given safely and breathing is monitored.

options.text: Choose and give an anticonvulsant of your own choice from the ward stock.
options.feedback: The choice of medicine is a prescriber or protocol decision.
options.consequence: An unsuitable medicine is given and the team has to correct it.

options.text: Refuse to prepare anything and wait for the doctor to do everything.
options.feedback: Refusing to prepare authorised emergency care delays treatment of a continuing seizure. Work within competency and protocol, and summon appropriate assistance immediately.

steps.info: The seizure has not stopped after the first treatment.

observations.label: Blood glucose
observations.value: Initial check requested; confirm result or obtain urgently if still unavailable

options.text: Seek expert guidance urgently, confirm the initial glucose result or obtain it if still unavailable, reassess breathing and give further emergency treatment only under the authorised pathway.
options.feedback: Failure of initial seizure treatment requires urgent expert guidance. Confirm that reversible causes such as hypoglycaemia were assessed early; reassess if needed without delaying emergency treatment. NICE NG217 specifies a time-sensitive repeat benzodiazepine pathway when a convulsive seizure persists after first-line treatment, with expert guidance for subsequent treatment failure. Verify the exact drug, time and response of the first dose, maintain respiratory monitoring, and prepare the next authorised treatment without delay; the individual plan and emergency protocol determine administration.
options.consequence: Expert help is on its way and a treatable cause is not missed.

options.text: Give an extra dose from stock immediately without checking what was already given or following the emergency plan.
options.feedback: Do not give an unverified repeat dose. Further treatment may be urgently indicated, but confirm the initial medication and timing and follow the authorised emergency plan with respiratory monitoring.
options.consequence: Unverified repeat medication creates avoidable risk of respiratory depression and treatment error.

options.text: Assume the seizure will stop soon and stop observing the patient.
options.feedback: The patient needs continuous observation and escalation when treatment is not working.

learning_points: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is an emergency: call for help, note the time and start emergency care.
Anticonvulsant medicines are given only as prescribed or per the plan or protocol; the nurse prepares, gives per order and monitors breathing.
Check for treatable causes such as hypoglycaemia during the initial response without delaying emergency treatment. If the seizure continues, seek expert guidance and confirm the results.
Document the first treatment's agent, time and response; persistent convulsions require time-sensitive authorised escalation and continued respiratory monitoring.
